title: Beneath a Steel Sky review (1994)
author: Gary Whitta
text:
Special commentary on this classic PC Gamer review provided by:
From the archives: The review below appears as originally written, with only minor changes in formatting and screenshots. By Garry Whitta
Beneath a Steel Sky review – PC Gamer #1 (UK, December 1993)
It's here at last. After two years in development and more column inches of enthusiastic preview copy than is healthy, Revolution Software and Dave Gibbons' Beneath A Steel Sky, finally, arrives. And it couldn't be further removed from the Hull-based company's 1992 debut.
After the magic and mythology of Lure Of The Temptress comes an oppressive, futuristic techno-thriller that borrows heavily from the pioneering sci-fi works of Philip K Dick and William Gibson. Take one part of Blade Runner, add a generous helping of Gibbons' own Give Me Liberty graphic novel, season to taste with a little Total Recall, and you've got Beneath A Steel Sky in a nutshell.
(Image credit: PC Gamer) This review was originally published in PC Gamer #1 (UK, December 1993) .
You can still subscribe to PC Gamer to get new issues of the magazine (in print!) every month.
Depending on how cynical you are, Beneath A Steel Sky's concept is either a brilliantly conceived piece of science fiction or just a plagiarised compilation of existing sci-fi ideas. Set in the near future, the world government has collapsed and corrupt corporations are now free to take control of the planet.
As the global ecology is ravaged by pollution, the upper-class nouveau riche retreat underground, while the less well-off are forced to live and work in claustrophobic towers high above the surface. Beyond all this is The Gap, a desert outland populated by those who refuse to live in the city—and also home to our hero, Robert Foster, a raincoat-clad hunk propelled into the story after the sinister police kidnap him from his home without explanation and a subsequent helicopter crash leaves him stranded, totally alone, in the higher reaches of the towering city.
But to give away any more of the story here would be to spoil one of the game's strongest aspects. Apart from a few clues delivered during the intro, Beneath A Steel Sky deliberately gives you hardly any information about why you've been kidnapped, what you have to do, or even where you are at the outset. Half the fun is to be had unravelling the mystery and watching the plot slowly unfold as you go.
To be honest, Beneath A Steel Sky is pretty conventional in its approach—despite what you may have heard. As an adventure game there's nothing radically original on offer. It is big though (around 100 locations), and features countless puzzles and a myriad of genuinely interesting characters. A particularly nice touch is your robotic companion, Joey, a decidedly wise-ass robot who, although starting the game as a lowly circuit board, can be plugged into all manner of cybernetic bodies to help you perform helpful tasks. The well-scripted love-hate relationship between the two characters really helps bring them both to life.
Progress in Beneath A Steel Sky is about getting to the bottom of things in more ways than one—starting near the top of the city, you'll have to get to the surface and ultimately underground in order to solve the mystery and crack the main conspiracy. Along the way, there are security forces to avoid, an all-powerful central computer to contend with and numerous sub-plots and red herrings to divert your attention. The game is still basically about using the right object in the right place at the right time, but it's compelling because it's so richly plotted and well thought out from beginning to end. Serious adventure hacks will be in hog heaven.
Counterpoint
What do you best remember about the Monkey Island games? More than likely, it's not the graphics (ace though they are) or the easy-to-get-to-grips-with interface (icon of user friendliness though it may be). No, it's probably the jokes.
You know, the spitting contest, the bit where his trousers fall down... And that for me, is where Beneath A Steel Sky falls down. It's just not funny. (It's not even trying to be funny most of the time.) Okay, it's not really fair to complain when a game fails to provide something it never set out to do in the first place (this is much more your Indiana Jones & The Fate Of Atlantis than your Sam And Max) but consider—LucasArts haven't done a serious adventure in a long time. And why? Because the funny ones are more popular, that's why.
That's not to say more serious graphic adventures can't work—this one, on the whole, is pretty, involving, well-constructed and, in most areas, just plain good —but simply that a few jokes would have spiced things up a bit.
—Matt Bielby
But the game's not without its faults. The main problem I have is that it doesn't seem to know quite what tone it should set. From what you've heard, and what you're shown during the introduction sequence, you'd have every right to expect a dark, gloomy and atmospheric vision of a sleazy, corrupt future. However, no matter how hard Gibbons' beautifully-realised background artwork and truly excellent accompanying mini-comic try to set the mood, there are too many distracting factors at work here that dilute the effect.
Maybe it's that I just can't take the little on-screen characters seriously enough to care for them or, in the case of the numerous baddies, feel threatened by them. Maybe it's because the music, which should have been as haunting and ominous as the powerful graphics, mostly consists of a series of inappropriate themes which at times sound more like jolly Radio One jingles.
In reality, probably all these things are to blame—the game simply spreads itself too thin, trying to be at once wildly atmospheric, comedic, menacing and tongue-in-cheek.
No matter how close it may come at times, Beneath A Steel Sky never quite manages to immerse you in a brooding, sinister world the way the designers obviously intended. But then again I'm probably just being a jaded bastard. The game may be very pretentious, but should we really take it that seriously? This isn't a movie or a high-brow novel, it's a computer game, for God's sake, and although it may have its failings as a piece of interactive fiction, as an adventure game in the classic LucasArts tradition it's difficult to find fault with.
In fact, it's at least as good—although not as funny—as anything that LucasArts has come up with in the last year. But as for the hyped claim that it's "The World's First Computer-Based Animated Comicbook Adventure," well, I'm still far from convinced. Just take Beneath A Steel Sky for what it is and not for what it may otherwise pretend to be and you'll have a whale of a time.

title: This remarkable mod transforms the most frightening horror game of the decade into Mirror's Edge
author: Rick Lane
text:
Amnesia: The Bunker is without a doubt the most frightening horror game I've played this decade. Its terrifying tale of being chased through a crumbling French bunker by a monster has the darkest, thickest, most unnerving atmosphere of any horror game I've played since Alien: Isolation . It's so intense that it's hard to imagine anyone making something light and airy out of its subterranean warrens, and it's downright inconceivable that someone might, say, turn Amnesia: The Bunker into Mirror's Edge.
And yet, that's exactly what modder TiMan has done. Created for Frictional Games' 2026 modding jam —which ran with the theme of 'What is reality?'— Bunker's Edge sees the base game's protagonist Henri transported through a portal from the trenches of war-ravaged France to the pristine skyline of EA's free-running classic.
The change of scenery alone is remarkable. The Bunker's HPL engine is purpose built to deliver darkness, shadows and murk, so seeing it handle such a bright and colourful environment is mightily impressive. But what's really interesting is how TiMan has implemented all of Mirror's Edge's free-running mechanics. Mantling, sliding, wall-running, pipe-climbing, runner's vision, that 180-degree wall-jump that I always struggled to perform in the base game, it's all here.
Despite the breezier setting, Bunker's Edge is still a horror game. The Bunker's monster has followed Henri through the portal, and chases him across the rooftops just as relentlessly as it stalks him through the base game's subterranean fortification.
All told, it's a snazzy bit of modding showmanship, though there are a couple of points to be aware of. First off, Bunker's Edge is (very understandably) not as slick as actual Mirror's Edge. Some of Henri's parkour moves, like sliding, are a little awkward, and more than once I clambered straight through a wall and found myself trapped inside the world geometry.
The other thing to note is that Bunker's Edge is very short. You can blast through the whole thing in about 15 minutes. The ending is also extremely weird, not what you'd expect from either The Bunker or Mirror's Edge.
Nonetheless, Bunker's Edge is a fun diversion for a Sunday afternoon. Alongside hosting modding jams, Frictional is also working on its next horror game Ontos . The sci-fi adventure has more in common with 2015's Soma than The Bunker, but it's still one of my most anticipated games of 2027.

title: As an OG Crazy Taxi lover, its new remake might just not be crazy enough
author: Mollie Taylor
text:
I've played just about every damn iteration of Crazy Taxi there is. My first exposure to it was the PlayStation 2 EyeToy version included in Sega Superstars, which involved me wildly gesticulating and yelling in order to get Axel's attention. Yes, for some reason you are the passenger in the EyeToy version of Crazy Taxi. I don't know either.
Then I spent a fair bit of time behind the wheel in both its Dreamcast and arcade versions—we don't talk about the myriad of mobile travesties—so I was pretty jazzed about the announcement of Crazy Taxi: World Tour. I was promptly un-jazzed by all the generative AI discourse that mired the hours following its reveal trailer, but you know.
(Image credit: Sega) Allegedly its use remains firmly in the conceptual stages of development, which I still don't love, but I was determined to not let that cloud my opinion of the game as I sat down to give it a whirl at Gamescom. And honestly? After an hour, I kinda felt like that was all the time I needed with Crazy Taxi: World Tour. As much as I wanted to be sold on a modern-day iteration, I'm just not quite there yet.
My time with the demo popped me behind the wheel as Crazy Taxi poster boy Axel, and dropped me into its thematically-appropriate Germany map. There'll be five cities with the full release, but I imagine most of what I saw in the game's amalgamation of various German cities will be true of the rest of the game.
The traditional Crazy Taxi time-attack style of picking up and dropping off as many passengers as possible is still here, and can be initiated at pretty much any time by stopping in their vicinity. Arguably the more fun part of World Tour, though, are the various side quests and challenges you can undertake. I stumbled (or coasted, I guess) past one that required me to drive around with a whole bunch of pizzas stacked in my back seat, while another one had an adrenaline junkie tag along as I drove off a huge ledge at high speed before coming to a breaking stop below, launching them into the air.
(Image credit: Sega) Each of these challenges comes with a star rating slapped onto them—the better I perform, the higher the rating. Pretty simple stuff. The problem is, beyond that, I didn't actually find driving around in Crazy Taxi all that fun. Drifting doesn't quite have that juice to it, and handling feels a lot tighter than it did in the original game, but that's to its detriment.
I also just don't love the way Crazy Taxi: World Tour looks. It has this awfully cheap quality to it, one that feels devoid of any real identity. It doesn't have that wonderful cartoonishness of the original that I'd immediately recognise as a game from Sega's catalogue. It looks like the kind of game that had generative AI heavily involved in its conceptual process. Which as we've already established, it does.
World Tour includes the zany Offspring songs of the original, real-life brands (the Puma store is back in World Tour) and Axel's wild green spiky 'do, but it's wrapped up in an utterly sauceless presentation, one that not even a relatively impressive recreation of Cologne's gothed-out-the-wazoo cathedral can save.
It sucks, because I would absolutely persevere through Crazy Taxi's duller driving portions in favour of seeing it bring real-world locations to life, but as it stands? I'm just not feeling it. I'll be keeping a watchful eye from the sidewalk, but I'm certainly not itching to hop back into the driver's seat of this Crazy Taxi any time soon.

title: Upcoming vampire RPG Nighthawks has been removed from Steam search and delisted in certain countries as Valve classifies it Adults Only: 'It's very bad news for us'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Nighthawks , the long-in-development vampire RPG due to be released later this month, is the latest game to run afoul of Steam's increasingly stringent rules regarding adult content. According to publisher Wadjet Eye Games, the game has been labelled 'Adults Only'—causing it to be removed from Steam search and outright delisted in certain countries like Germany—despite claims from both developer and publisher that the RPG's depictions of sex and nudity are very mild.
"We are aware that Steam has classified Nighthawks as an adult game and has excluded it from searches," Wadjet Eye boss Dave Gilbert wrote on Bluesky . "We are working on it. Valve is under the impression that this game is way sexier than it actually is." Gilbert further commented that "Valve is basically treating Nighthawks like a porn game!" in responding to a reply to his initial post.
A game being labelled Adults Only can affect its visibility in several ways. Adults Only games will not appear in Steam searches by default, requiring users to log in, verify their age (which requires the use of a credit card in some countries) and adjust their preferred content settings before they become visible. In addition, the label can cause games to be delisted outright in certain countries.
In a statement to PC Gamer, Nighthawks' creator Richard Cobbett (who, for the sake of transparency, is also a PC Gamer contributor) provided an overview of the situation, and how the Adults Only label is likely to affect Nighthawks' launch:
"It's very bad news for us, because it immediately makes the game persona non grata in several important countries like Germany," Cobbett wrote. "We're not sure exactly what triggered the issue, but we've obviously contacted Valve and we're hoping that they will quickly remove the scarlet letter."

However, regarding nudity, sex, and similar elements specifically, it's really all very mild, usually comedic in tone when it happens, and far less explicit than anything you'd see on HBO."

Nighthawks isn't the only game to be recently caught out by Valve's stricter adult content policies. In July, the indie adventure Future? No thanks! was forced to delay its release on account of a weeks-long Steam review process, which was triggered by the presence of 'dozens of untextured polygons depicting ass and boobs' in one of its sequences. The review process was eventually completed in the game's favour, and Future? No Thanks! released on Steam on September 4.
Part of the problem is that Valve's rules on what qualifies as adult content are somewhat byzantine . Valve requires developers to appropriately age gate games with mature or adult themes, but doesn't itself draw a line between the two, requiring developers to make that judgment for themselves. Matters were further complicated last year when Valve added another rule that prohibits "Content that may violate the rules and standards set forth by Steam’s payment processors and related card networks and banks, or internet network providers. In particular, certain kinds of adult only content."
Ultimately, Cobbett concluded that "If you're not scandalised by the likes of Dragon Age , you're really not going to get too hot and bothered here either. We're hoping that Valve will quickly reverse the decision and approve the game so that everyone can get to be the vampire they deserve to be as planned next week."

title: Ashly Burch, voice of Horizon's Aloy and star of Mythic Quest, is currently obsessed with Slay the Spire 2 and thinks videogames have too many stoic characters: 'I want more sh*tty little b*tches'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Disk Cleanup
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"
Ashly Burch's first encounter with PC gaming was playing a Donkey Kong knockoff on a PC her mother had bought to practice typing. But the first PC game that truly resonated with her was LucasArts' Day of the Tentacle : "That was the first time I played a game that I can remember that had a narrative and comedy," she says. "It was one of those things where, when you're younger, you find something that expands your concept of what a thing can be."
Burch came to the world's attention through the online, gaming-themed sketch show Hey Ash, Whatcha Playin' , before making her videogame acting debut as Tiny Tina in Borderlands 2. Since then, Burch's roles have included Chloe in Life is Strange , Parvati Holcomb in The Outer Worlds , and Aloy in Guerrilla Games' Horizon series.
More recently, Burch returned to sending-up videogames in Apple TV's game-development comedy Mythic Quest , and is currently working on her passion project I'm Happy You're Here —a YouTube comedy series that explores coping with mental health issues: "They're easy, shareable, hopefully easy to understand distillations of complicated concepts, and yeah, they're all for free on YouTube," she says. "It's something I've wanted to make for a long time."
Burch took a break from puppet psychotherapy to show me around her Steam library. We deliberated the benefits of notebooks in detective games, vetted cosy gaming's dating profiles, and discussed the secret sauce behind Slay the Spire.
What game are you currently playing?
(Image credit: William Rous, Evil Trout) The Incident at Galley House . I just started playing yesterday. It's brand new. I'm at that part that I think happens with every detective game, where you're like, "I have too many leads".
I'm overwhelmed. I resist having a notebook at first when I do detective games, and inevitably I have to cave and start physically writing stuff down. I did that with Blue Prince . I had a massive notebook for [that], and Lorelei and the Laser Eyes , I had to have a massive notebook for that.
Why do I resist it? Is it laziness? It might be laziness. There's a part of me that's like, "It's fun that a game is complex enough that you have to keep your own personal notes." And then there's another part of me that's like, "But shouldn't that all be internal to the system?" Like, shouldn't whatever mechanism you need to track things be housed within the game? But there's no rule for that.
I love detective games. I think the first one I fell in love with was Return of the Obra Dinn . And then I think when I played Chants of Sennaar , I was like, "This is my new favourite genre." It often felt like adventure games could be a bit arbitrary. It wasn't necessarily logic that would lead you to the solution for something. It might be brute forcing, just being like, "I don't know where the fuck I'm going—rubber chicken on every single thing that I find."
When it's a good detective game, you really feel like a detective. You really are putting clues together and creating logical connections … and especially in Return of the Obra Dinn, when you get things correct, you're like, "I'm a genius".
What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?
(Image credit: NPC Studio) I just uninstalled it because I put too many hours into this game, and I can't look at the little icon anymore. It was Fields of Mistria .
I usually seek out cosy games when I'm using my brain a lot in my day-to-day, if I'm in a writer's room or I just feel like my brain is full of too much stuff. I will do a cosy game to just zone out.
What I really liked about it is that I find sometimes in cosy games, if there are romance options, there's like two characters with distinct personalities, and everyone else is the same. They might have different hobbies, but they don't fundamentally feel like different people. And I feel what Fields of Mistria did well is that—and it's not perfect, I still think there's a handful of characters that feel similar—but more than most games, I would say half the characters are distinct.
And the other thing that's interesting—this is a strange compliment—but they managed to capture the kids very, very well. There's three kids in the village, and they're maybe the most interesting.
A difficult thing with writing is that often people feel like their characters are distinct because they have certain backstories or they have certain interests, but if you don't pull those things forward and have them affect the way that they speak, the way that they act, they way that they move, they don't end up feeling different. I think often games can fall into that trap. These characters look, even just aesthetically, they look really different, so that should be enough. And it's like, well, you have to write them differently. I really liked that about Mistria
What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?
(Image credit: Cardboard Computer) I mostly play on my Steam Deck. I think the oldest game currently installed on my Steam Deck is Kentucky Route Zero . Don't take my gamer card away, I never finished it. That's why it's installed, because I was looking through my library and being like, "What games do I need to give another crack at?"
I was a lot younger because [it was] 13 years ago, and I think I just couldn't latch onto the abstract David Lynch-y vibe of it. I think I was more impatient with games too back in the day. And also since 2020 I've become a reader. I didn't really read books very much before 2020. I was just so tired of looking at screens that I was like, "I have to put my eyes anywhere else."
So now, I think I've built up more patience and attention span, frankly, from reading. I am curious about how I would feel going back into Kentucky Route Zero now that my frontal lobe is completely developed.
What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?
(Image credit: Mega Crit) Fields of Mistria isn't as bad as I thought. Slay the Spire 2 is as bad as I thought—270 hours. I got really obsessed. I loved Slay the Spire very much, and then, actually I'm curious because I don't just play PC. I'm all over the place and I don't have my old Xbox anymore. I wonder if Spelunky would have more hours? Probably.
But yeah, it was one of those things where I would be like, "Well, I'm waiting for this thing, I'll do a run." Then there were definitely nights where I was like, "I have to get to Ascension 10" and do 10 hours or something. I would like to say that part of it is because it has co-op, and I played a lot of co-op, but I haven't played that much co-op. Most of those are singleplayer hours.
It's such a well-designed roguelike. I mean, Slay the Spire 2 is still in early access obviously, so it's not as tight necessarily as Slay the Spire 1. But it's still quite comparable. And it's so addictive too. It has this thing of the luck and skill are in perfect balance in that game. It's the consolidation of many, many different, smart choices that make it a good game. And I don't think you can point at any one main mechanic or something.
The other thing—it's such a small thing—but what I really love is that, again, it's the thing of distinct characters, you get the idea of who these people are through how they play. There are these little sprinkles of characterisation that just make it feel fuller. Like the Regent is a new character, and he's sort of a prissy, shitty king. It took me many playthroughs to realise that the throne he's sitting in is being held up by two little minions whose legs are constantly shaking because they're having trouble holding him up. That is such a fun little detail, you get so much information about who this guy is from just looking at him.
I think we can get trapped in, with games, this stoic, cool character [archetype]. There's a lot of stoic, cool, badass characters. You know what I mean? So when there's a shitty little posh prince, I'm like, "Yes! Give me more of that." I want more shitty little bitches.
What game will you never, ever uninstall?
(Image credit: Riot Games) It's probably League of Legends because I play ARAM with friends. I haven't played in a minute. I need to get back on it. But for a while that was my after-work ritual—I would get on with a few friends and we'd play a couple of games of ARAM.
I remember being in a group chat with them or something [during the pandemic] and they were like, "You should learn [League] because what the fuck else are we going to do right now?" Which I'm glad about because it's so much to learn. And truly I would not have been able to if we were not in a global pandemic and I had time to do it. I just don't like the number of characters, and they're always releasing new champions, and then you have to know how the champions work, and then you need to understand all the items, and thank god I don't have to worry about runes anymore. But now I have the hang of enough champions, and I know enough about how the other ones work, that I can hold my own.
What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?
(Image credit: Musegroup) This is kind of a lame answer, but I have Audacity , which is how I record my voice auditions, and I've used it now for so many years that I'm sure I could use a different program. I just don't want to because I'm not doing anything complicated.
How tidy is your desktop screen?
Quite tidy. There's a draft of something I'm working on. So on the left side of the screen, I have like two documents and Fade In . Oh, I guess this is another answer to your previous question. I don't use Final Draft for writing scripts, I use Fade In. So this is probably another program that I would never uninstall.
Final Draft is so expensive, and it feels like every two years they force you to update and then force you to buy it again or something. Fade In is like, I think when I bought it, it was like $60, and then you're done. I don't know how they make money, frankly. And it's like the same thing with Audacity, which is like I just need you for script format. That's all.
I can't handle clutter. When I start to write something, especially, the space around me has to be clean or I can't focus. And if my house gets too cluttered it's the same thing. I have to be tidy before I can do anything else. I do have OCD, so that might be why … it really calms my nervous system down.

title: Inzoi's director says he is 'very much focused on our core goals' as he announces a multiplayer roleplaying mode designed to be like Ready Player One
author: Rick Lane
text:
We all hoped that Inzoi would be the competitor to The Sims 4 that the life sim genre has needed for years. Thus far, though, things haven't quite panned out that way. Life sim expert Mollie Taylor described Inzoi's early access version as a "shallow imitation" of The Sims, while the game's own director Hyungjin "Kjun" Kim conceded that building a life sim has proven much harder than he anticipated .
Since then, Kim has spent the last year working on new features for InZoi, which I personally hope will result in a much richer simulation. But in his latest Steam update , Kim's focus was on something entirely different. Alongside the base game, Kim is apparently working on a whole new way to play called 'Canvastown'.
This essentially lets players roleplay as a single character in the town, rather than overseeing everyone's lives from a bird's-eye view. "The main goal of Canvastown is to get away from mundane daily life and capture memorable moments within life simulation so you can jump in and enjoy only those extraordinary moments", Kim explained.
The mode will allow players to create their own Zoi and customise their house, before entering an dedicated online space called 'AR Company' that allows "around 50 people" to "converse and interact in the same channel under mutual consent." So it's essentially a mini online village populate by players, although Kim says that NPC Zois will appear in these spaces too. "Like a movie director, you can assign roles and cast your actors to create your scenario."
He adds that players will be able to further enhance their Canvastown through using "script mods" that will let players "create mini-game like car racing". Kim doesn't specify whether players will be able to create such script mods, but does state that he hopes these mini-games "can later be added to the main game as well".
Kim cites the movie Ready Player One as an example of the kind of experience he's trying to build, stating he wants players to be able to "step away from reality into this world of Inzoi where they can live out a different life."
It also sounds like it'll be a while before players will get their hands on it. "Looking at the current build makes me sigh. There are so many lacking areas, and we have a very long way to go." He also emphasises that Canvastown is a "side project" and that Inzoi Studio is "very much focused on our core goals."
It all sounds very ambitious, but I do wonder whether Kim is trying to run before he can walk. As he's stated in the past, making a standard, run-of-the-mill life simulation is not easy, and I wonder whether it may have been better to keep this side project under wraps until Inzoi had really nailed the fundamentals. This is doubly important considering that Inzoi now has some stiff competition in Paralives , which according to Mollie made a considerably stronger early access debut .

This essentially lets players roleplay as a single character in the town, rather than overseeing everyone's lives from a bird's-eye view. "The main goal of Canvastown is to get away from mundane daily life and capture memorable moments within life simulation so you can jump in and enjoy only those extraordinary moments", Kim explained.

The mode will allow players to create their own Zoi and customise their house, before entering an dedicated online space called 'AR Company' that allows "around 50 people" to "converse and interact in the same channel under mutual consent." So it's essentially a mini online village populate by players, although Kim says that NPC Zois will appear in these spaces too. "Like a movie director, you can assign roles and cast your actors to create your scenario."

He adds that players will be able to further enhance their Canvastown through using "script mods" that will let players "create mini-game like car racing". Kim doesn't specify whether players will be able to create such script mods, but does state that he hopes these mini-games "can later be added to the main game as well".

Kim cites the movie Ready Player One as an example of the kind of experience he's trying to build, stating he wants players to be able to "step away from reality into this world of Inzoi where they can live out a different life."

It also sounds like it'll be a while before players will get their hands on it. "Looking at the current build makes me sigh. There are so many lacking areas, and we have a very long way to go." He also emphasises that Canvastown is a "side project" and that Inzoi Studio is "very much focused on our core goals."

It all sounds very ambitious, but I do wonder whether Kim is trying to run before he can walk. As he's stated in the past, making a standard, run-of-the-mill life simulation is not easy, and I wonder whether it may have been better to keep this side project under wraps until Inzoi had really nailed the fundamentals. This is doubly important considering that Inzoi now has some stiff competition in Paralives, which according to Mollie made a considerably stronger early access debut.

title: Peacock’s Friday the 13th Prequel Is Already Looking Like a Must-Watch

text: This October is shaping up to be a great time for fans of horror on TV. American Horror Story is returning with a massive crossover in its thirteenth season . title: 原创｜3年不见，暴雪憋大招：2款炸裂新作、多款史诗更新……这阵仗久违了
author: 零
text:
文｜游戏那点事｜零
今天一大早，安纳海姆会议中心外就排起了长队。晨光穿过棕榈树，广场上站满了等候入场的玩家。
（清晨的安纳海姆会议中心外）
（场馆外围等候入场的玩家）
距离上一届暴雪嘉年华，已经过去近三年。重新聚到这里，玩家们显然攒了不少期待。
进入会场，大屏幕还在倒计时，舞台前已经举起了一片手机。
（开幕式开始前，观众已经举起手机等待）
站上舞台的Johanna Faries，也迎来了自己出任暴雪娱乐总裁后的第一届嘉年华。她特别说起，自己过去就参加过这场聚会，只是第一次以现在的身份来到台前。能够再一次与来自世界各地的玩家相聚，让她颇为感慨。
（暴雪娱乐总裁Johanna Faries）
谈到《风暴英雄》，Johanna讲起了筹备期间的一件事：她曾告诉团队，如果没有这款游戏的实质消息要分享，自己就不来参加嘉年华了。
紧接着播放的预告，揭晓了《风暴英雄》这次带来的新消息：萨拉塔斯将作为远程刺杀型英雄加入时空枢纽。画面中，她从虚空传送门中缓缓降下，熟悉的身影很快点燃了现场。按照此次公布的海外日程，她将于9月14日进入公开测试服（PTR），9月28日正式上线。
（萨拉塔斯从虚空传送门中现身）
Johanna也向一直为这款游戏发声的玩家致谢：“谢谢你们一直相信这款游戏。”她说，大家持续传递着这份热情，也不断提醒暴雪，这款游戏对他们意味着什么——“有时候，声音还相当大”。
这只是开场。接下来，《星际争霸》公布开放世界射击新作，《暗黑破坏神5》正式揭晓；《守望先锋》《炉石传说》带来新英雄、新职业与新玩法；《魔兽争霸III》续写战役，《魔兽世界》则在正式服、怀旧服之外，开启了一段新的冒险。随着消息陆续揭晓，掌声和欢呼也一轮接着一轮响起。
从眼前就能玩到的更新，到未来数年的新作，这场开幕式接连给出了惊喜，也把一个问题重新带到我们面前：那个我们熟悉的暴雪，回来了吗？
一、《星际争霸》的新篇章，从开放世界射击开始
从即时战略走向开放世界射击，是《星际争霸》新作的最大变化。这次游戏的名称就是“STARCRAFT”，以科普卢星区为背景，计划于2030年春推出。
登台介绍新作的Dan Hay强调，游戏会尊重这个系列原有的基调，同时尝试新的表达方式。过去，玩家从高处指挥战争；这次，他希望把人带到地面，“置身泥泞与战火”。
开幕式上公布的CG《Dominion》，也沿着一名普通士兵的经历展开——他宣誓、受训，一次次获得勋章，带着自豪与期待准备奔赴战场。陆战队员的动力装甲在车间里展开，把这个年轻人装进了我们熟悉的战争机器。
（车间里的陆战队员动力装甲）
随后，兵营降落，虫群涌来。身边的战友接连倒下，手中的步枪却在紧要关头报错。那些在即时战略游戏（RTS）里不断被生产、派出和消耗的单位，在这里有了惊恐的面孔。
（运送陆战队员的兵营降落在战场）
影片的结尾，残破的装甲重新回到车间。工人拾起血污中的勋章，随手丢进已经堆满勋章的回收箱。等待维修的装甲排成一列，新的士兵还会继续到来。征兵宣传里的荣誉与现实中的消耗，形成了《星际争霸》熟悉的黑色讽刺。
（从战场送回车间的动力装甲，已经浸满血污）
对《星际争霸》而言，转向射击游戏最值得关注的，正是Dan Hay所说的视角变化：玩家将从指挥军队的人，变成置身战场的人。CG已经用一名陆战队员的经历，展示了这种讲述战争的方式。不过，目前公布的信息仍以类型、世界观和推出时间为主，开放世界如何展开、射击玩法如何设计，还要等待后续展示。
二、血律登场、黑影转职，《守望先锋》的年度故事走向终章
《守望先锋》公布了今年的第九名新英雄、游戏的第54位英雄——血律。他是一名来自津巴布韦的支援英雄，将于10月7日随国服第5赛季正式加入。开幕式结束后，线上玩家也能参与英雄限时试玩。
在登场预告《越狱》中，末日铁拳与盟友潜入“监测站：格里姆火山”，救出这位相识多年的老朋友，并希望借助他的力量打造新的拳套。
（《越狱》中的血律）
血律的设计围绕吸血鬼展开：汲取敌人的生命力，操纵蝙蝠外形的无人机，手中的权杖既能治疗队友，也能伤害敌人。他最特别的机制，是强化下一次技能。游戏总监Aaron Keller在台上举了一个直观的例子：原本用来冲刺的技能，强化后就能变为飞行。玩家需要根据战况，把强化留给适合当下的技能。
与此同时，黑影和路霸将迎来重做。黑影从输出转为支援，保留冲锋手枪、传送和黑客能力，同时获得持续治疗指定队友，以及在区域内治疗队友、削弱敌人的手段。路霸则可以吸收敌方投射物，将其压缩为爆炸废料球再打出去。
（黑影重做后的技能组）
英雄之外，血律登场预告中的冰岛监狱“监测站：格里姆火山”也将成为新地图。“心动先锋”带来新的皮肤与漫画，LE SSERAFIM的新一轮游戏内联动则已上线。
这次的新英雄和地图，也延续着年度故事“黑爪之治”。叙事负责人Miranda Moyer在台上回顾，斩仇击败末日铁拳、夺取黑爪领导权后，开始向全球扩张；而末日铁拳并未死去，如今正召集盟友准备归来。第5赛季将为这段故事收官，第6赛季则为明年的剧情铺垫。
“英雄是我们一切创作的核心。”Aaron Keller在介绍中如此概括。随着第6赛季最后一名新英雄推出，年初公布的十名新英雄计划也将完成。开幕式已经展示了十名角色的合影，最后一位的更多细节将在今年晚些时候公开。
下一场“精彩聚焦”发布活动定在2027年2月，届时将介绍新故事、英雄与系统。从今年的安排来看，《守望先锋》正以年度剧情组织多次赛季更新：新角色与地图既带来玩法，也承接动画中发生的故事。玩家对一个角色的关注，由此可以从看预告延续到参与新赛季。
三、《暗黑破坏神5》揭晓，亚马逊也在路上
《暗黑破坏神》系列迎来30周年，暴雪在这次开幕式上公布了下一代作品：《暗黑破坏神5》计划于2029年春推出。
“英雄们已经不在，庇护之地已经陷落，迪亚波罗已经获胜。”负责介绍新作的Joe Shely，用这几句话交代了故事的起点。
（《暗黑破坏神5》预告中的庇护之地）
这一次，玩家进入的世界已经落入迪亚波罗之手。Joe Shely希望围绕生存、力量与代价展开新的故事，并在台上提出了一个问题：“当世界已经陷落，你必须变成什么？”
本次开幕式的展示以故事设定为主，尚未展开介绍具体职业和系统。
《暗黑破坏神4》的后续更新安排，也在这次开幕式上公布。
暴雪在今天宣布，第15赛季将从北京时间9月16日0:30起陆续开放，以系列30周年为主题。迪卡·凯恩会带领玩家重访经典场景，三大魔神也将登场。玩家需要收集它们的灵魂碎片，选择拥抱哪一种力量，并承担相应的代价。
Joe Shely还在现场拿出了Nintendo Switch 2，宣布《暗黑破坏神4》将登陆这一平台，海外发售日为9月15日。此次公布的合集包含本体，以及《憎恨之躯》《憎恨之王》两部资料片。
（Switch 2版合集将收录本体与两部资料片）
再往后，系列经典职业亚马逊也将加入《暗黑破坏神4》。
随着《憎恨之王》把玩家带到斯科沃斯群岛，这个与当地紧密相连的经典职业，也成为玩家关注的对象。Tiffany Wat在台上说起，玩家踏上群岛之后，一直在追问同一个问题：“亚马逊在哪里？”这次暴雪确认，亚马逊将以独立职业包的形式回归，计划于2027年上半年推出。
（亚马逊的标枪与盾牌概念图）
亚马逊会使用弓作战，也将把标志性的标枪作为新武器类型带入《暗黑破坏神4》。
《暗黑破坏神：不朽》则公布了与《再生侠》（Spawn）的联动。
系列也将走向游戏之外：暴雪正与Netflix开发一部《暗黑破坏神》动画剧集，尚未公布播出日期。
在下一代作品到来之前，《暗黑破坏神4》仍会通过赛季与职业包继续增加可玩的内容，Switch 2版则让它进入新的主机平台。对一个走过30年的系列来说，这次发布既关乎如何继续服务现有玩家，也关乎怎样通过新作与动画，把庇护之地带给更多人。
四、武僧、拼装与双人组队，《炉石传说》还有新花样
《炉石传说》一口气公布了新扩展、新随从类型、日志改版与双人乱斗，并在最后揭晓第12个职业——武僧。
先登场的是“黑暗帝国的统治”，国服将于10月21日上线。这次，故事回到艾泽拉斯的远古，上古之神尚未被囚禁，我们熟悉的世界也还未成形。克苏恩、恩佐斯、尤格-萨隆和亚煞极统治着腐化的大地，与泰坦造物的大军交战。
（上古之神统治下的远古艾泽拉斯）
新关键词“拼装”把这种混乱带进了牌局：将一张随从牌置入手牌后，使用特定随从池中另一张随从的文本，替换这张牌的部分文本，从而组合出新的效果。它有明确的随从池与替换范围，同时为卡牌之间的配合增加了变数。
（“拼装”效果的组合示意）
酒馆战棋也将加入“畸变怪”这一全新随从类型。它们围绕弃牌联动积蓄力量，试图唤醒所信仰的上古之神；每有一个畸变怪死亡，这个时刻就会更近一步。
变化还会发生在牌局之外。
主菜单将加入新的导航栏，日志也会改版。任务、成就和活动将与扩展故事联系起来，玩家的旅程会按周推进。执行制作人Nathan Lyons-Smith解释，他们希望“每一次来到旅店，都像是在参与一段更大的冒险”，让玩家在打牌之外，也能持续感受到故事的进展。
（开幕式用一张“日志”卡牌揭晓这次改版）
乱斗模式还将尝试2对2：两名玩家组队，对抗另一支双人队伍。平时各自打牌的朋友，也有了并肩作战的新选择。
随后，陈·风暴烈酒在动画中现身，揭晓了计划于2027年3月登场的武僧职业。
（陈·风暴烈酒将作为武僧英雄加入旅店）
Brenden Sewell介绍，武僧的特点是敏捷、灵活，能够根据牌局变化调整打法，并在合适的时机打出连招。更多细节将在明年年初公开。
对一款已经积累了大量卡牌和玩法的产品来说，这批更新同时触及了三个层面：新职业与“拼装”扩充对局变化，双人乱斗增加共同游玩的方式，日志则把分散的任务与活动串进持续推进的故事。
五、决战萨拉塔斯之外，《魔兽世界》开启“无限”冒险
《魔兽世界》这次带来了两组重要消息：正式服即将迎来“至暗之夜”的收尾，经典怀旧服团队则公布了全新项目《魔兽世界》：“无限”。
2023年的嘉年华上，暴雪一口气公布了“世界之魂传说”的三部资料片，如今这个三部曲已走到中段。计划于2027年年初推出的12.2“临界蚀刻”，将是“至暗之夜”的最后一次大型内容更新。
游戏总监Ion Hazzikostas说，过去一段时间，故事一直在为终局布置棋子；接下来，直到整个三部曲结束，剧情都会全速向前。萨拉塔斯已经接近自己的目标，玩家也终于要与她正面交锋。
《一门之隔》揭晓预告片展示了她想要夺取的东西：艾泽拉斯的世界之魂。她试图与其合而为一，玩家必须前往世界深处，阻止这一切发生。
（萨拉塔斯与艾泽拉斯的世界之魂）
新区域“地幔宝库”由泰坦建造，已经尘封数千年。玩家会在这里探索全新巢穴“齿轮堡”，提升新阵营“辉光之核”的名望，并参与“辉光悲鸣”引发的区域事件。
（地幔宝库概念图）
新的团队副本“世界之核”设有八名首领。玩家需要突破防御、击败萨拉塔斯的副官，最终与她交手。攻克团队副本后，还能开启“至暗之刃”的任务线。这把法系匕首，是“世界之魂传说”的首件传说武器。
第3赛季也准备了不同规模的挑战：史诗钥石轮换池由八座地下城组成，其中包括拥有三名首领的新地下城“斯雷加的据点”；地下堡的新宿敌则是阿斯塔洛·血誓。圣骑士还将开放暗夜精灵、被遗忘者和暗矛巨魔三种种族选择。
第三部资料片“最后的泰坦”也展示了新的前瞻画面。这个在2023年便已公布的项目，将于明年初公开更多信息。短片《撼世之威》的结尾，风雪中逐渐显现出一个巨大的身影，预示着接下来的威胁。
（《撼世之威》片尾的巨型身影）
而“无限”，给出了另一种重返艾泽拉斯的方式。
“是的，这就是Classic Plus。”执行制作人Holly Longdale在台上确认。这个由经典怀旧服团队开发的新项目，将与正式服、怀旧服并列，成为《魔兽世界》的第三种体验。它保留原版的冒险节奏，同时持续开发新的区域、任务、地下城与系统，让经典时代的艾泽拉斯继续生长。
（“无限”的全新区域河林）
其中最关键的安排，是等级上限将长期维持在60级，玩家的冒险进度持续保留。
Holly解释，团队不希望大家不断向前赶，把已有的成就、装备和朋友留在身后。未来的成长，会通过新故事、新体验和持续更新来实现。
“重要的是旅程，而不是终点。”她反复强调，在这里不需要急着追赶。
首批内容包括三个新区域、1000多个全新任务、九座新地下城和两座新团队副本。玩家可以探索河林，踏上海加尔山，也会在原有区域发现未曾涉足的地点。新种族天裔是一群高等精灵流亡者，可以选择加入联盟或部落。
（对抗阿克蒙德的大战，仍在海加尔山留下痕迹）
此外，游戏还将开放被遗忘者圣骑士、矮人萨满祭司等种族职业组合，并更新天赋树、装备与物品。玩家还可以根据账号下所有角色取得的进度，获得账号共享奖励；营火功能则让玩家在旅途中更容易结识同伴。
画面升级包括全局光照、体积雾、水面反射和地形阴影等效果，整体仍会保留原版的美术风格。
（“无限”内容预览中的光照与水面效果）
“无限”将于11月5日在国服上线。拥有有效的《魔兽世界》游戏时间即可游玩；购买天裔史诗礼包，可以获得10月6日开启的国服Beta测试资格。天裔种族及其起始区域，则属于相应礼包内容。
正式服与“无限”，面对的是玩家对《魔兽世界》的不同期待。前者沿着连续资料片走向三部曲终局，不断展开新的高等级挑战；后者则把经典时代的冒险节奏保留下来，并向各个等级阶段持续增加内容。等级上限固定在60级，意味着开发者需要在既有世界中创造新的成长与探索空间；玩家在升级途中经过的地方，也有机会成为值得长期停留的目的地。
六、23年后，《魔兽争霸III》再续战役
《魔兽争霸III》同样拿出了新的故事，而且开幕式当天就已推出。
“被遗忘者王国”是这个系列时隔逾23年的首个全新战役，包含一个序章与三个章节，带来超过30小时的全新剧情。
故事从洛丹伦的陷落讲起。泰瑞纳斯国王死于阿尔萨斯之手，天灾军团继续北上，王国与人民则被留在废墟之中。新战役关注的，是这些被复活为亡灵的人，如何挣脱控制、重新获得自由意志，并为夺回家园而战。
（“被遗忘者王国”预告中的战争场面）
玩家将亲历洛丹伦沦陷，在地下墓穴中建立幽暗城，逐渐积蓄力量，迎战血色十字军与天灾军团中的新仇旧敌。希尔瓦娜斯等熟悉角色也会出现。
Holly Longdale在介绍中提出，玩家将通过这段经历，理解“成为被遗忘者究竟意味着什么”。对熟悉《魔兽世界》的玩家而言，幽暗城与被遗忘者早已是这个世界的一部分；新战役则让这段历史重新成为可以亲手推进的RTS冒险。
（“被遗忘者王国”预告片尾的亡灵身影）
与战役一同到来的，还有3.0更新。已有《魔兽争霸III：重制版》的玩家可以免费获得这次更新，“被遗忘者王国”则需要单独购买。
新的中立英雄“被遗忘者圣骑士”，将向所有《魔兽争霸III》玩家开放，不限版本。终极版画面升级会提高地形、建筑与角色单位的精细度，保留原有的等距俯视视角，并允许玩家在终极版与原版画面之间切换。
世界编辑器也会改善地形塑造、光照运用与操作便利性，方便地图作者继续制作对战地图和不同的游戏模式。
（3.0版本的世界编辑器）
《魔兽争霸III》的生命力，长期来自官方内容与玩家自制地图的共同支撑。新战役提供了一段由暴雪创作的冒险，编辑器的改进则服务于仍在创作的地图作者。
七、那个我们熟悉的暴雪，回来了吗？
从开场的《风暴英雄》到最后的《魔兽世界》：“无限”，这场开幕式反复回应着老玩家的期待。对Johanna来说，这也是她出任总裁后，第一次在嘉年华上集中展示暴雪准备如何经营这些系列。
她此前接受采访时提到，希望以五年为尺度规划旗下系列，让整个暴雪每年持续交付一至两项重大内容。她认为，现有的游戏世界仍有许多值得探索的空间；提前明确方向，也能让开发与非开发团队更早围绕同一计划展开工作。
这次嘉年华，让这样的规划有了具体的呈现。《风暴英雄》的新英雄、《魔兽争霸III》的新战役，回应了老玩家长期以来的期待；《星际争霸》尝试新的游戏类型，“无限”则在经典玩法的基础上增加新冒险。
与此同时，几款持续运营的游戏，也给出了各自的更新安排。《守望先锋》年初提出的年度叙事与十名新英雄计划正在推进，《魔兽世界》继续走向已公布的三部曲终局，《暗黑破坏神》则将近期赛季、明年职业包与下一代作品一并呈现。玩家由此能知道下一次回来的理由，也能看到更远一些的开发方向。对暴雪而言，把更新提前排好、再按计划做出来，是重新建立期待与信任的一部分。
影视方向同样有了新的进展。此前接受采访时，Johanna还没有给出具体项目；本次开幕式上，与Netflix合作开发的《暗黑破坏神》动画剧集已经正式公布。她在台上说：“我们不只是暴雪游戏，我们是暴雪娱乐。”
（开幕式上公布的《暗黑破坏神》动画项目）
这些变化足以让人对暴雪多一些期待。但熟悉的名字与漂亮的预告，终究还要变成玩家愿意长期投入的作品。老系列尝试新类型，能否把积累多年的世界观转化为有吸引力的玩法？年度更新与更长的项目规划，能否保持质量、按期兑现？“那个我们熟悉的暴雪，回来了吗？”这个问题，还要在接下来的游戏里寻找答案。
至少在这一天，从清晨会场外的长队，到开幕式上一轮又一轮的掌声与欢呼，玩家们对这些世界的热爱依然清晰可见。
